title: attention-memory-slice-powercurve-profiling
content:
Purpose / TL;DR:
- Explore a memory-slicing approach (split attention into smaller memory-resident tiles) to avoid OOMs and reduce GC/peak-memory pressure for long sequences while keeping latency acceptable.
- Compare three attention execution strategies: FlashAttention2 (monolithic kernel), Paged-attention (paged KV + tiling), and Fused-ops (attention fused with layernorm/ffn microkernels).
- Produce power/latency curves across sequence lengths (64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1536, 2048) and batch sizes (1,2,4) on A100-80GB and H100-80GB.

Context / why this matters:
- We keep seeing customer apps hit OOM or sudden latency spikes when sequence length distribution has a heavy tail (some requests at 2k tokens).
- FlashAttention is great for short-medium seq (<=1024) but sometimes fails gracefully for long sequences under reserved pools because of memory fragmentation and transient spikes.
- Paged approaches can trade off extra copies/indirections for lower peak resident memory and better steady-state throughput.
- Fused ops reduce kernel launch overhead for small tokens but show weird tail-latency regressions when combined with dynamic KV cache usage.

Hardware/Environment:
- Nodes: 4x A100-SXM4-80GB (driver 535.54), CUDA 12.2, PyTorch 2.2 with Triton 2.0, kernel build from branch: gpu/attention-profiling-v3.
- Also ran subset on H100 (driver 535.54, CUDA 12.2) to check SM/warp sched differences.
- Docker image: redwood/serving-bench:2024-11-01 (includes perf tooling).
- Profiler tools used: nvprof-like metrics via Nsight Systems (nsys), nvtx markers + cupy/cuda event timers, and torch.profiler aggregated traces.

Models tested:
- small: 7B (bfloat16, no quant) mimic Llama-7B spec
- med: 13B (int8/4bit experiments disabled for baseline)
- microbench framework: synthetic transformer block that isolates single attention call with configurable seq_len, head_count, head_dim.

Experiment design notes (rough):
- For each (seq_len, batch, model) do: 20 warmup iterations + 200 measured iterations; record mean latency, p50/p90/p99, GPU Memory high-water mark, CUDA kernel timeline.
- Two modes: cold-start (no KV cache), streaming (incremental tokens appended where KV cache grows) to capture repeated kernel launches on growing cache.
- Evaluate two scheduling policies: continuous-batching (we pack up to N tokens across requests) and single-request scheduling (no cross-request batching) to measure worst-case tail.

Memory-slicing idea (short):
- Split Q/K/V compute into S slices along sequence dimension so each slice fits comfortably in device memory budget. Compute attention for slice pairs and accumulate outputs.
- Benefits: lower instantaneous peak allocation; can prevent OOM and reduce GC from allocations collateral.
- Cost: more kernel launches, extra temporary buffers for partial accumulations, slightly higher total compute due to boundary handling.

Key experiment runs (summarized):
- Test matrix: seq = [256,512,1024,1536,2048], batch=1, head_dim=128, heads=16.
- R1 FlashAttention baseline (no memory slicing).
- R2 Paged-attention (page size tuned: 256 tokens/page).
- R3 Memory-slice (slice sizes tried: 128, 256, 512).
- R4 Fused-ops attention (attention fused w/ residual+ln microkernel).

Observed notes (raw):
- seq<=512: FlashAttention wins in latency and p99. Kernel durations dominated by a single big attention kernel (flash_cuda_attention) with high SM utilization (~85%). Small number of kernel launches (<=6) per forward.
- seq in [1024,1536]: Flash shows steadily rising peak memory; occasional slowdown due to CUDA out-of-memory retries in our reserved environment. Paged-attention shows flatter memory curve; latency slightly higher but p99 more stable.
- seq=2048: Flash baseline often hits OOM in tight memory environment; paged-attn and memory-slice both complete. Memory-slice with slice=512 achieves ~1.15x latency vs paged but uses 25% less peak memory.
- Fused-ops: for seq<=256 fused wins (fewer kernel launches). For seq>=1024 fused regresses—profiling shows lots of small kernels with low occupancy (~25–30%) and high scheduler overhead.

Representative numbers (batch=1, 7B, A100):
- seq 512: Flash: mean 21.4ms, p99 34.0ms, mem 28.5GB. Paged: mean 26.1ms, p99 36.7ms, mem 20.1GB. Slice(256): mean 24.7ms, p99 35.9ms, mem 18.9GB.
- seq 1024: Flash: mean 46.0ms, p99 88.2ms, mem 41.2GB (OOM attempts in 2/10 runs). Paged: mean 55.6ms, p99 62.3ms, mem 30.2GB. Slice(512): mean 51.2ms, p99 59.8ms, mem 29.4GB.
- seq 2048: Flash: OOM. Paged: mean 138.5ms, p99 182.2ms, mem 58.3GB. Slice(512): mean 126.8ms, p99 149.1ms, mem 43.7GB.

Profiling excerpts (nsys / nvtx observations):
- FlashAttention kernel: large single kernel, high SM efficiency, long duration. But when memory pressure increases we saw device-to-host fallback allocations in allocator trace (~2–3ms stalls) which correlate to p99 spikes.
- Paged-attn timeline: series of repeated small kernels performing page loads + attention on each page. Host->device page transfer (pinned memcpy) overlapped well with compute for large pages, leading to steady throughput.
- Memory-slice: increased number of kernel launches ~ (num_slices * base_kernels). Slice boundary accumulation produces small extra kernel for reduction. Slicing improved allocator behavior (less fragmentation events in allocator traces).
- Fused-ops: observed numerous tiny kernels converting layout + fused-ops; SM occupancy low and many back-to-back launches causing CPU driver overhead.

Hypotheses / interpretation:
1) Peak memory is the primary failure mode for Flash on longer sequences; avoiding big monolithic allocations (via paging or slicing) makes system more stable in shared reserved environments.
2) Paged approach has slightly higher per-token overhead but offers best p99 stability in production-like multi-tenant settings.
3) Memory-slice is a good compromise: lower peak than Flash and lower latency than Paged in our tests if slice size is tuned.
4) Fused-ops need rework: fusion should aim to reduce kernel count while preserving occupancy—current implementation over-fuses into many micro-kernels. Consider multi-stage fusion with larger tiles.

Actionable follow-ups / TODOs:
- [ ] Run same matrix on H100 and report relative delta; early H100 runs show 10–15% lower kernel latency but similar memory dynamics. (assigned: Tom)
- [ ] Add simulated multi-tenant load (concurrent small + large requests) to measure allocator fragmentation and evictions. (assigned: Priya)
- [ ] Try hybrid: paged-attn for KV storage + memory-sliced compute in each page; aims to combine best of both worlds. Implement prototype in branch hybrid/paged-slice. (assigned: Marco)
- [ ] Investigate allocator behavior: reproduce with environment variable MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD-like tuning for CUDA caching allocator; capture allocator debug logs. (assigned: Aisha)
- [ ] Measure power/energy per token (wall time * average power draw) to quantify cost tradeoffs — add nvidia-smi polling in bench harness.

Notes on tuning knobs tried:
- page_size: values 128/256/512 tested; 256 had best overlap of memcpy+compute on A100.
- slice_size: 128 gives lowest peak memory but too many kernel launches; 512 reduces launches but peak memory increases; 256 appears sweet spot for 7B configs.
- prefetching: prefetch next page overlapped with current compute reduced p99 by ~8% for paged-attn.
- cudaGraph: attempted capture for Flash; graph capture reduced CPU overhead for repeated calls but didn't help with allocator fragmentation.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How do these results change with int8/4-bit quantized models where attention math has smaller memory footprint but different kernel characteristics?
- Can we expose slice/page sizing as an adaptive policy at runtime (based on free memory + sequence length) without user intervention?
- For long streaming sessions (many steps) does paged approach yield better amortized throughput over time? Need longer-run experiments (1k+ steps).

Repro commands (example):
- baseline flash: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python perf/attention_microbench.py --model 7b --seq_len 1024 --heads 16 --head_dim 128 --impl flash --iters 200 --warmup 20 --nvtx
- paged: python perf/attention_microbench.py --impl paged --page_size 256 --prefetch true --nvtx
- slice: python perf/attention_microbench.py --impl slice --slice_size 256 --nvtx
- collect nsys: nsys profile --sample=cpu --trace=cuda,osrt --output run_seq1024_flash nsys_run.sh

Links / references (work/PRs):
- github PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/578 (paged-attn prototype)
- jira: INF-4321 attention OOM spikes incident notes
- confluence draft: serving-runtime/attention-optimizations (high-level proposal)

Appendix: quick sketch of memory-slice algorithm (informal)\- for start in 0..seq step slice_size:
  - load Q_slice/K_slice/V_slice (compute Q,K,V for tokens in that slice)
  - for previous slices (or global K_cache pages) compute cross-attn partials where required
  - do attention for slice vs page pairs and accumulate to output buffer
  - write back or stream out partial outputs
  - reduction step to finalize overlapped contributions

Notes-to-self / scribbles:
- consider exposing metrics: allocator_fragmentation_events, peak_alloc_events, average_temp_alloc_size in Console per model/route
- reputation risk: long-tail p99 impacts customer SLAs -> prefer stable paged/sliced default for models >13B or seq>1024 in Dedicated clusters
- grooming item: create an RFC for hybrid/paged-slice with cost model and safety fallbacks (OOM -> switch to paged automatically)

End.
